title: AI complaints swamp practice staff and hit morale, poll shows
source_used: The Independent (GPonline original returned 403; LBC carries the same text)
key_facts: The Medical Protection Society (MPS), which gives legal and indemnity advice to health workers, says GPs are being sent AI-assisted complaint letters that can run to 20 pages or longer.
MPS surveyed nearly 160 UK practice managers: only 7% had never received an AI-generated complaint.
45% said patient complaints drafted with AI are adding to workload pressures and damaging staff morale and wellbeing.

MPS deputy medical director Dr Sarah Townley says AI can help patients who struggle to write, but the letters are often complicated, include 'occasionally questionable' legal arguments and may divert time from patient care; she says low effort may also lower the threshold for complaining.

Royal College of GPs president Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown says complaints matter for accountability, but AI may produce unnecessarily lengthy or inaccurate ones and GPs also face complaints reflecting wider NHS pressures.
The Public Service Ombudsman has issued guidance for patients using AI to write complaints: plain language helps more than formal or legal wording, and AI providers may use personal information.
quote_evidence: A survey of nearly 160 UK practice managers revealed that just 7 per cent have never received an AI-generated complaint.
Meanwhile, 45 per cent stated that patient complaints drafted with AI are compounding workload pressures and damaging staff morale and wellbeing.
Letters can be 20 pages, sometimes longer.
why_it_matters_hint: AI makes it quick to write long complaints, which may slow replies and take practice time from patient care, though the evidence is a survey of about 160 managers.
notes: GPonline (the pool item) returned HTTP 403, so the text was read on The Independent (published 11 Oct 2026 23:03 GMT) and cross-checked against LBC (12 Oct 2026), whose text is near-identical (possibly shared agency copy; not confirmed). The figures come from the MPS survey; sample size is 'nearly 160' and no polling dates or method are given.
